claim: Deficiency of coenzyme Q (CoQ) is necessary and sufficient for insulin resistance in adipocytes and skeletal muscle.
source: Previously we showed that deficiency of coenzyme Q (CoQ) is necessary and sufficient for IR in adipocytes and skeletal muscle (Fazakerley et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Fazakerley et al., 2018).

claim: Elevated levels of ceramide in the mitochondria of skeletal muscle cells result in CoQ depletion.
source: We demonstrate that elevated levels of ceramide in the mitochondria of skeletal muscle cells result in CoQ depletion and loss of mitochondrial respiratory chain components, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and IR.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including measurements of ceramide and CoQ levels in mitochondria.

claim: Elevated levels of ceramide in the mitochondria of skeletal muscle cells result in loss of mitochondrial respiratory chain components.
source: We demonstrate that elevated levels of ceramide in the mitochondria of skeletal muscle cells result in CoQ depletion and loss of mitochondrial respiratory chain components, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and IR.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data showing depletion of respiratory chain components upon ceramide elevation.

claim: Elevated levels of ceramide in the mitochondria of skeletal muscle cells lead to mitochondrial dysfunction and insulin resistance.
source: We demonstrate that elevated levels of ceramide in the mitochondria of skeletal muscle cells result in CoQ depletion and loss of mitochondrial respiratory chain components, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and IR.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing impaired mitochondrial respiration and insulin resistance upon ceramide elevation.

claim: Decreasing mitochondrial ceramide levels in vitro increased CoQ levels and was protective against insulin resistance.
source: Further, decreasing mitochondrial ceramide levels in vitro and in animal models (mice, C57BL/6J) (under chow and high-fat diet) increased CoQ levels and was protective against IR.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell culture experiments showing increased CoQ and protection from insulin resistance.

claim: Decreasing mitochondrial ceramide levels in animal models (mice, C57BL/6J) under chow diet increased CoQ levels and was protective against insulin resistance.
source: Further, decreasing mitochondrial ceramide levels in vitro and in animal models (mice, C57BL/6J) (under chow and high-fat diet) increased CoQ levels and was protective against IR.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mouse studies showing increased CoQ and protection from insulin resistance.

claim: Decreasing mitochondrial ceramide levels in animal models (mice, C57BL/6J) under high-fat diet increased CoQ levels and was protective against insulin resistance.
source: Further, decreasing mitochondrial ceramide levels in vitro and in animal models (mice, C57BL/6J) (under chow and high-fat diet) increased CoQ levels and was protective against IR.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mouse studies showing increased CoQ and protection from insulin resistance.

claim: CoQ supplementation rescued ceramide-associated insulin resistance.
source: CoQ supplementation also rescued ceramide-associated IR.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that CoQ supplementation reversed insulin resistance induced by ceramides.

claim: There is a strong correlation between the respirasome system and mitochondrial ceramide as key determinants of insulin sensitivity in human muscle.
source: Examination of the mitochondrial proteome from human muscle biopsies revealed a strong correlation between the respirasome system and mitochondrial ceramide as key determinants of insulin sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic analysis of human muscle biopsies showing correlations between respirasome components, ceramide levels, and insulin sensitivity.

claim: Insulin is the primary hormone responsible for lowering blood glucose by stimulating glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissue.
source: Insulin is the primary hormone responsible for lowering blood glucose, in part, by stimulating glucose transport into muscle and adipose tissue.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about insulin function.

claim: Insulin-stimulated glucose transport is mediated by the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/Akt-dependent delivery of insulin-sensitive glucose transporters (GLUT4) to the plasma membrane.
source: This is mediated by the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/Akt-dependent delivery of insulin-sensitive glucose transporters (GLUT4) to the plasma membrane (PM) (Hill et al., 1999; Cong et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Hill et al., 1999; Cong et al., 1997).

claim: The process of insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation is defective in insulin resistance.
source: This process is defective in insulin resistance, a significant risk factor for cardiometabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (James et al., 2021), heart failure (Riehle and Abel, 2016), and some types of cancer (Leitner et al., 2022), and so defective GLUT4 translocation represents one of the hallmarks of insulin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (James et al., 2021; Riehle and Abel, 2016; Leitner et al., 2022).

claim: Insulin resistance is a significant risk factor for type 2 diabetes.
source: This process is defective in insulin resistance, a significant risk factor for cardiometabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (James et al., 2021), heart failure (Riehle and Abel, 2016), and some types of cancer (Leitner et al., 2022), and so defective GLUT4 translocation represents one of the hallmarks of insulin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (James et al., 2021).

claim: Insulin resistance is a significant risk factor for heart failure.
source: This process is defective in insulin resistance, a significant risk factor for cardiometabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (James et al., 2021), heart failure (Riehle and Abel, 2016), and some types of cancer (Leitner et al., 2022), and so defective GLUT4 translocation represents one of the hallmarks of insulin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Riehle and Abel, 2016).

claim: Insulin resistance is a significant risk factor for some types of cancer.
source: This process is defective in insulin resistance, a significant risk factor for cardiometabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (James et al., 2021), heart failure (Riehle and Abel, 2016), and some types of cancer (Leitner et al., 2022), and so defective GLUT4 translocation represents one of the hallmarks of insulin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Leitner et al., 2022).

claim: Defective GLUT4 translocation represents one of the hallmarks of insulin resistance.
source: This process is defective in insulin resistance, a significant risk factor for cardiometabolic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (James et al., 2021), heart failure (Riehle and Abel, 2016), and some types of cancer (Leitner et al., 2022), and so defective GLUT4 translocation represents one of the hallmarks of insulin resistance.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The development of insulin resistance in skeletal muscle and adipocytes has been associated with mitochondrial coenzyme Q (CoQ) deficiency.
source: The development of insulin resistance in skeletal muscle and adipocytes has been associated with multiple intracellular lesions, including mitochondrial coenzyme Q (CoQ) deficiency (Fazakerley et al., 2018a), accumulation of intracellular lipids such as ceramides (Holland and Summers, 2008), and increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Anderson et al., 2009; Hoehn et al., 2009; Fazakerley et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Fazakerley et al., 2018a).

claim: The development of insulin resistance in skeletal muscle and adipocytes has been associated with accumulation of intracellular lipids such as ceramides.
source: The development of insulin resistance in skeletal muscle and adipocytes has been associated with multiple intracellular lesions, including mitochondrial coenzyme Q (CoQ) deficiency (Fazakerley et al., 2018a), accumulation of intracellular lipids such as ceramides (Holland and Summers, 2008), and increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Anderson et al., 2009; Hoehn et al., 2009; Fazakerley et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Holland and Summers, 2008).

claim: The development of insulin resistance in skeletal muscle and adipocytes has been associated with increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: The development of insulin resistance in skeletal muscle and adipocytes has been associated with multiple intracellular lesions, including mitochondrial coenzyme Q (CoQ) deficiency (Fazakerley et al., 2018a), accumulation of intracellular lipids such as ceramides (Holland and Summers, 2008), and increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Anderson et al., 2009; Hoehn et al., 2009; Fazakerley et al., 2018b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Anderson et al., 2009; Hoehn et al., 2009; Fazakerley et al., 2018b).

claim: CoQ is a mitochondrial cofactor and antioxidant synthesized and localized in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM).
source: CoQ (CoQ9 in rodents and CoQ10 in humans) is a mitochondrial cofactor and antioxidant synthesized and localized in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CoQ.

claim: CoQ9 is the form of coenzyme Q found in rodents.
source: CoQ (CoQ9 in rodents and CoQ10 in humans) is a mitochondrial cofactor and antioxidant synthesized and localized in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CoQ.

claim: CoQ10 is the form of coenzyme Q found in humans.
source: CoQ (CoQ9 in rodents and CoQ10 in humans) is a mitochondrial cofactor and antioxidant synthesized and localized in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CoQ.

claim: CoQ is essential for mitochondrial respiration.
source: This cofactor is essential for mitochondrial respiration (Hatefi et al., 1962), fatty acid oxidation (Frerman, 1988), and nucleotide biosynthesis (Jones, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Hatefi et al., 1962).

claim: CoQ is essential for fatty acid oxidation.
source: This cofactor is essential for mitochondrial respiration (Hatefi et al., 1962), fatty acid oxidation (Frerman, 1988), and nucleotide biosynthesis (Jones, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Frerman, 1988).

claim: CoQ is essential for nucleotide biosynthesis.
source: This cofactor is essential for mitochondrial respiration (Hatefi et al., 1962), fatty acid oxidation (Frerman, 1988), and nucleotide biosynthesis (Jones, 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Jones, 1980).

claim: Mitochondrial, but not global, CoQ9 depletion is both necessary and sufficient to induce insulin resistance in vitro and in vivo.
source: We reported that mitochondrial, but not global, CoQ9 depletion is both necessary and sufficient to induce insulin resistance in vitro and in vivo (Fazakerley et al., 2018a), suggesting a causal role of CoQ9/10 depletion in insulin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Fazakerley et al., 2018a).

claim: CoQ deficiency can result from primary mutation in the CoQ biosynthetic machinery (named complex Q).
source: CoQ deficiency can result from primary mutation in the CoQ biosynthetic machinery (named complex Q) (Montini et al., 2008) or secondary from other cellular defects such as deletion of the oxidative phosphorylation system (OXPHOS) (Kühl et al., 2017; Calvo et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Montini et al., 2008).

claim: CoQ deficiency can result secondary from other cellular defects such as deletion of the oxidative phosphorylation system (OXPHOS).
source: CoQ deficiency can result from primary mutation in the CoQ biosynthetic machinery (named complex Q) (Montini et al., 2008) or secondary from other cellular defects such as deletion of the oxidative phosphorylation system (OXPHOS) (Kühl et al., 2017; Calvo et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kühl et al., 2017; Calvo et al., 2020).

claim: Low levels of CoQ10 are associated with diabetes.
source: Low levels of CoQ10 are associated with human metabolic disease, including diabetes (Ates et al., 2013; El-ghoroury et al., 2009), cardiovascular disease (Zozina et al., 2018), and aging (de Barcelos and Haas, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ates et al., 2013; El-ghoroury et al., 2009).

claim: Low levels of CoQ10 are associated with cardiovascular disease.
source: Low levels of CoQ10 are associated with human metabolic disease, including diabetes (Ates et al., 2013; El-ghoroury et al., 2009), cardiovascular disease (Zozina et al., 2018), and aging (de Barcelos and Haas, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Zozina et al., 2018).

claim: Low levels of CoQ10 are associated with aging.
source: Low levels of CoQ10 are associated with human metabolic disease, including diabetes (Ates et al., 2013; El-ghoroury et al., 2009), cardiovascular disease (Zozina et al., 2018), and aging (de Barcelos and Haas, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (de Barcelos and Haas, 2019).

claim: Many conditions associated with low CoQ10 levels are also associated with loss of OXPHOS and mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: Strikingly, many of these conditions are also associated with loss of OXPHOS and mitochondrial dysfunction (Højlund et al., 2010; Diaz-Vegas et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Højlund et al., 2010; Diaz-Vegas et al., 2020).

claim: Ceramides belong to the sphingolipid family.
source: Ceramides belong to the sphingolipid family, and high levels are strongly associated with insulin resistance (Chaurasia and Summers, 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about ceramides.

claim: High levels of ceramides are strongly associated with insulin resistance.
source: Ceramides belong to the sphingolipid family, and high levels are strongly associated with insulin resistance (Chaurasia and Summers, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Chaurasia and Summers, 2021).

claim: It has been proposed that ceramides cause insulin resistance by inhibition of PI3K/Akt signaling.
source: While it has been proposed that ceramides cause insulin resistance by inhibition of PI3K/Akt signaling (Summers et al., 1998; Schubert et al., 2000; Powell et al., 2003), there is now considerable evidence that does not support this (Fazakerley et al., 2018a; James et al., 2021; Kono and Barham, 1971; Hoehn et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Summers et al., 1998; Schubert et al., 2000; Powell et al., 2003).

claim: There is considerable evidence that does not support the proposal that ceramides cause insulin resistance by inhibition of PI3K/Akt signaling.
source: While it has been proposed that ceramides cause insulin resistance by inhibition of PI3K/Akt signaling (Summers et al., 1998; Schubert et al., 2000; Powell et al., 2003), there is now considerable evidence that does not support this (Fazakerley et al., 2018a; James et al., 2021; Kono and Barham, 1971; Hoehn et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Fazakerley et al., 2018a; James et al., 2021; Kono and Barham, 1971; Hoehn et al., 2008).

claim: Ceramides may induce insulin resistance by a non-canonical mechanism.
source: Hence, ceramides may induce insulin resistance by a non-canonical mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the evidence that ceramides do not act through PI3K/Akt signaling.

claim: N-acetylsphingosine (C2-ceramide) causes rapid decline of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in isolated mitochondria.
source: The rapid decline of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in isolated mitochondria in the presence of N-acetylsphingosine (C2-ceramide), a synthetic ceramide analog that can penetrate cells, suggests that ceramides may be responsible for defective mitochondria (Di Paola et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Di Paola et al., 2000).

claim: The effect of ceramides on mitochondrial respiration seems to be ceramide-specific as neither diacylglycerides (DAGs) nor triacylglycerides (TAGs) affect mitochondrial respiration.
source: This effect seems to be ceramide-specific as neither diacylglycerides (DAGs) nor triacylglycerides (TAGs) affect mitochondrial respiration (Perreault et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Perreault et al., 2018).

claim: Reducing mitochondrial, but not global, ceramide in the liver protects against the development of diet-induced insulin resistance and obesity.
source: Recent evidence suggests a link between mitochondrial ceramides and insulin sensitivity, with the observation that reducing mitochondrial, but not global, ceramide in the liver protects against the development of diet-induced insulin resistance and obesity (Perreault et al., 2018; Hammerschmidt et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Perreault et al., 2018; Hammerschmidt et al., 2019).

claim: Mitochondrial ceramide levels are more strongly associated with insulin resistance than with whole-tissue ceramide in human skeletal muscle.
source: Consistent with this, mitochondrial ceramide levels are more strongly associated with insulin resistance than with whole-tissue ceramide in human skeletal muscle (Perreault et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Perreault et al., 2018).

claim: No direct evidence exists linking mitochondrial ceramides with insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle.
source: Despite this association, no direct evidence exists linking mitochondrial ceramides with insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Incubation of L6 myotubes with palmitate (150 μM for 16 hr) reduced the insulin-stimulated translocation of GLUT4 to the cell surface by ~30%.
source: As shown (Figure 1A), incubation of L6 myotubes with palmitate (150 μM for 16 hr) reduced the insulin-stimulated translocation of GLUT4 to the cell surface by ~30%, consistent with impaired insulin action.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Palmitate treatment of L6 myotubes did not cause any defect in proximal insulin signaling as measured by phosphorylation of Akt or TBC1D4.
source: Despite this marked defect in GLUT4 translocation, we did not observe any defect in proximal insulin signaling as measured by phosphorylation of Akt or TBC1D4 (Figure 1C and D – 100 nM insulin; 20 min).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: C2-ceramide inhibited both GLUT4 translocation and Akt phosphorylation in L6 myocytes.
source: Intriguingly, we were able to replicate that C2-ceramide inhibited both GLUT4 translocation and Akt phosphorylation in L6 myocytes (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Palmitate-induced insulin resistance was prevented by the ceramide biosynthesis inhibitor myriocin.
source: However, this is unlikely as palmitate-induced insulin resistance was prevented by the ceramide biosynthesis inhibitor myriocin (Figure 1A) and we observed a specific increase in C16-ceramide levels in L6 cells following incubation with palmitate, which was also prevented by myriocin (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Palmitate treatment of L6 cells caused a specific increase in C16-ceramide levels.
source: However, this is unlikely as palmitate-induced insulin resistance was prevented by the ceramide biosynthesis inhibitor myriocin (Figure 1A) and we observed a specific increase in C16-ceramide levels in L6 cells following incubation with palmitate, which was also prevented by myriocin (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Myriocin prevented palmitate-induced increase in C16-ceramide levels in L6 cells.
source: However, this is unlikely as palmitate-induced insulin resistance was prevented by the ceramide biosynthesis inhibitor myriocin (Figure 1A) and we observed a specific increase in C16-ceramide levels in L6 cells following incubation with palmitate, which was also prevented by myriocin (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: C2-ceramide does not faithfully recapitulate physiological insulin resistance, in contrast to that seen with incubation with palmitate.
source: Based on these data, we surmise that C2-ceramide does not faithfully recapitulate physiological insulin resistance, in contrast to that seen with incubation with palmitate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing different effects of C2-ceramide and palmitate on insulin signaling.

claim: CoQ9 supplementation overcame insulin resistance in palmitate-treated L6 myotubes.
source: Addition of CoQ9 had no effect on control cells but overcame insulin resistance in palmitate-treated cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CoQ9 supplementation had no impact on palmitate-induced ceramide accumulation.
source: Notably, the protective effect of CoQ9 appears to be downstream of ceramide accumulation, as it had no impact on palmitate-induced ceramide accumulation (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Both myriocin and CoQ9 reversed palmitate-induced insulin resistance.
source: Strikingly, both myriocin and CoQ9 reversed insulin resistance, suggesting that there might be an interaction between ceramides and CoQ in the induction of insulin resistance with palmitate in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that both treatments reversed insulin resistance.

claim: Palmitate lowered mitochondrial CoQ9 abundance by ~40%.
source: As shown (Figure 1G), palmitate lowered mitochondrial CoQ9 abundance by ~40%, and this was prevented with myriocin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Myriocin prevented palmitate-induced lowering of mitochondrial CoQ9 abundance.
source: As shown (Figure 1G), palmitate lowered mitochondrial CoQ9 abundance by ~40%, and this was prevented with myriocin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 4NB (2.5 mM for 16 hr) decreased mitochondrial CoQ9 to a similar extent as observed in palmitate-treated myocytes.
source: 4NB (2.5 mM for 16 hr) decreased mitochondrial CoQ9 to a similar extent as observed in palmitate-treated myocytes (Figure 1I) and generated insulin resistance in GLUT4-HA-L6 myotubes (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: 4NB (2.5 mM for 16 hr) generated insulin resistance in GLUT4-HA-L6 myotubes.
source: 4NB (2.5 mM for 16 hr) decreased mitochondrial CoQ9 to a similar extent as observed in palmitate-treated myocytes (Figure 1I) and generated insulin resistance in GLUT4-HA-L6 myotubes (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: 4NB-mediated insulin resistance was prevented by provision of CoQ9.
source: Notably, 4NB-mediated insulin resistance was prevented by provision of CoQ9, as described previously (Fazakerley et al., 2018a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior research (Fazakerley et al., 2018a).

claim: Total ceramide abundance was increased in 4NB-treated cells.
source: Interestingly, total ceramide abundance was increased in 4NB-treated cells, albeit to a lesser extent than observed with palmitate, without affecting other lipid species (Figure 1J and K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: Saclac (10 μM for 24 hr) reduced insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation by 40%.
source: Consistent with a role of ceramide in insulin sensitivity, Saclac (10 μM for 24 hr) reduced insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation by 40% (Figure 1L, vs Control; p<0.001), and this was prevented by myriocin or CoQ9 supplementation (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Myriocin prevented Saclac-induced reduction in insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation.
source: Consistent with a role of ceramide in insulin sensitivity, Saclac (10 μM for 24 hr) reduced insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation by 40% (Figure 1L, vs Control; p<0.001), and this was prevented by myriocin or CoQ9 supplementation (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: CoQ9 supplementation prevented Saclac-induced reduction in insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation.
source: Consistent with a role of ceramide in insulin sensitivity, Saclac (10 μM for 24 hr) reduced insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation by 40% (Figure 1L, vs Control; p<0.001), and this was prevented by myriocin or CoQ9 supplementation (Figure 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Saclac treatment did not cause detectable defects in Akt phosphorylation.
source: Notably, no detectable defects in Akt phosphorylation were observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Saclac increased total ceramide levels (approximately sixfold over basal) in HeLa cells.
source: Consistent with our observation in L6 myotubes, Saclac increased total ceramide levels (approximately sixfold over basal) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and lowered CoQ levels inside mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Saclac lowered CoQ levels inside mitochondria in HeLa cells.
source: Consistent with our observation in L6 myotubes, Saclac increased total ceramide levels (approximately sixfold over basal) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F) and lowered CoQ levels inside mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Myriocin prevented Saclac-induced-CoQ depletion in HeLa cells.
source: Of interest, myriocin prevented Saclac-induced-CoQ depletion, demonstrating that there is a similar interaction between ceramide and CoQ levels in this human cell line as observed in L6 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Doxycycline induced mitochondrial expression of mtSMPD5 in L6 cells.
source: As expected, doxycycline induced mitochondrial expression of mtSMPD5, as demonstrated by enrichment of SMPD5 in mitochondria isolated from L6 cells (Figure 2B), and this was associated with increased total mitochondrial ceramides to the same extent as observed with palmitate treatment (Figure 2C), with the largest increase in C16-ceramide (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mtSMPD5 overexpression increased total mitochondrial ceramides to the same extent as observed with palmitate treatment.
source: As expected, doxycycline induced mitochondrial expression of mtSMPD5, as demonstrated by enrichment of SMPD5 in mitochondria isolated from L6 cells (Figure 2B), and this was associated with increased total mitochondrial ceramides to the same extent as observed with palmitate treatment (Figure 2C), with the largest increase in C16-ceramide (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: mtSMPD5 overexpression caused the largest increase in C16-ceramide.
source: As expected, doxycycline induced mitochondrial expression of mtSMPD5, as demonstrated by enrichment of SMPD5 in mitochondria isolated from L6 cells (Figure 2B), and this was associated with increased total mitochondrial ceramides to the same extent as observed with palmitate treatment (Figure 2C), with the largest increase in C16-ceramide (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: mtSMPD5 overexpression did not affect ceramide abundance in the whole-cell lysate.
source: Importantly, mtSMPD5 overexpression did not affect ceramide abundance in the whole-cell lysate nor other lipid species inside mitochondria such as cardiolipin, cholesterol, and DAGs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and D–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: mtSMPD5 overexpression did not affect other lipid species inside mitochondria such as cardiolipin, cholesterol, and DAGs.
source: Importantly, mtSMPD5 overexpression did not affect ceramide abundance in the whole-cell lysate nor other lipid species inside mitochondria such as cardiolipin, cholesterol, and DAGs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and D–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–J.

claim: mtSMPD5 overexpression was sufficient to promote insulin resistance in response to submaximal and maximal insulin doses.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, mtSMPD5 was sufficient to promote insulin resistance in response to submaximal and maximal insulin doses (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: mtSMPD5 overexpression promoted insulin resistance without affecting Akt phosphorylation.
source: Furthermore, mtSMPD5 overexpression promoted insulin resistance without affecting Akt phosphorylation (Figure 2F–H), and no differences in total GLUT4 levels were observed across the treatments (Figure 2F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: Mitochondrial CoQ levels were depleted in both palmitate-treated and mtSMPD5-overexpressing cells without any additive effects.
source: In line with our previous results, mitochondrial CoQ levels were depleted in both palmitate-treated and mtSMPD5-overexpressing cells without any additive effects. This suggests that these strategies to increase ceramides share a common mechanism for inducing CoQ depletion in L6 myotubes (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: CoQ9 supplementation prevented both palmitate- and mtSMPD5-induced insulin resistance.
source: Importantly, CoQ9 supplementation prevented both palmitate- and mtSMPD5-induced insulin resistance (Figure 2J), suggesting that CoQ depletion is an essential mediator of insulin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Doxycycline increased the abundance of mtASAH1 in the mitochondrial fraction.
source: Doxycycline increased the abundance of mtASAH1 in the mitochondrial fraction, demonstrating the correct localization of this construct (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: mtASAH1 induction prevented palmitate-induced mitochondrial ceramide accumulation.
source: Furthermore, mtASAH1 induction prevented palmitate-induced mitochondrial ceramide accumulation (total levels and 18:1\16:0 ceramides) (Figure 3C), indicating that the enzyme was functioning as expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: mtASAH1 overexpression protected cells from palmitate-induced insulin resistance without affecting basal insulin sensitivity.
source: Notably, mtASAH1 overexpression protected cells from palmitate-induced insulin resistance without affecting basal insulin sensitivity (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: mtASAH1 overexpression did not rescue insulin sensitivity in cells depleted of CoQ.
source: Importantly, mtASAH1 overexpression did not rescue insulin sensitivity in cells depleted of CoQ (2.5 mM 4NB for 24 hr), supporting the notion that mitochondrial ceramides are upstream of CoQ (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: mtASAH1 overexpression increased CoQ levels.
source: Finally, mtASAH1 overexpression increased CoQ levels. In both control and mtASAH1 cells, palmitate induced a depletion of CoQ; however, the levels in palmitate-treated mtASAH1 cells remained similar to control untreated cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Treatment of adult mice with the CerS1 inhibitor P053 for 6 wk selectively lowered muscle ceramides without affecting other lipid species.
source: Treatment of adult mice with the CerS1 inhibitor P053 for 6 wk selectively lowered muscle ceramides without affecting other lipid species (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: CerS1 inhibition increased CoQ in mitochondrial fractions isolated from skeletal muscle.
source: Notably, CerS1 inhibition increased CoQ in mitochondrial fractions isolated from skeletal muscle (Figure 3K), and a similar effect was observed in mice exposed to an HFD for 5 wk (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Across control and mtSMPD5 cells, 2501 proteins were quantified where 555 were annotated as mitochondrial proteins.
source: Across control and mtSMPD5 cells, we quantified 2501 proteins where 555 were annotated as mitochondrial proteins (MitoCarta 3.0 and UniProt localization) (Rath et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data analysis.

claim: 9% of mitochondrially annotated proteins were significantly changed at 24 hr after mtSMPD5 overexpression.
source: Analysis of the proteome revealed that 9 and 19% of mitochondrially annotated proteins were significantly changed at 24 and 72 hr, respectively (adj. p<0.05, absolute log2 FC > 0.4), indicative of a temporal progression of changes following induction of mSMPD5 expression (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: 19% of mitochondrially annotated proteins were significantly changed at 72 hr after mtSMPD5 overexpression.
source: Analysis of the proteome revealed that 9 and 19% of mitochondrially annotated proteins were significantly changed at 24 and 72 hr, respectively (adj. p<0.05, absolute log2 FC > 0.4), indicative of a temporal progression of changes following induction of mSMPD5 expression (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Sixty proteins were decreased at 72 hr after mtSMPD5 overexpression, and of these 47% were functionally annotated as components of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source: Sixty proteins were decreased at 72 hr, and of these 47% were functionally annotated as components of oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS; rank 1, 28/135 proteins).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data analysis.

claim: Complex I (14/15 decreased), Complex III (5/6 decreased), and Complex IV (13/13 decreased) but not Complex II (0/3 decreased) or Complex V (3/15 decreased) were depleted after mtSMPD5 overexpression.
source: In this dataset, CI (14/15 decreased), CIII (5/6 decreased), and CIV (13/13 decreased) but not CII (0/3 decreased) or CV (3/15 decreased) were depleted after mtSMPD5 overexpression (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The assembly machinery associated with each complex was either upregulated or unchanged after mtSMPD5 overexpression.
source: Despite the bulk downregulation of CI, III, and IV, the assembly machinery associated with each complex was either upregulated or unchanged after mtSMPD5 overexpression (Figure 4J), suggesting that mitochondrial ceramides somehow alter ETC stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: mtSMPD5 overexpression decreased basal and ATP-linked mitochondrial respiration.
source: mtSMPD5 overexpression decreased basal and ATP-linked mitochondrial respiration (Figure 5A–C), as well as maximal, proton-leak and non-mitochondrial respiration (Figure 5A, D, E, and F), suggesting that mitochondrial ceramides induce a generalized attenuation in mitochondrial function.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: CoQ9 supplementation partially recovered basal and ATP-linked mitochondrial respiration in mtSMPD5-overexpressing cells.
source: Notably, we did not observe evidence of energy deficiency in our model (data not shown). Interestingly, CoQ9 supplementation partially recovered basal and ATP-linked mitochondrial respiration, suggesting that part of the mitochondrial defects are induced by CoQ9 depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: mtSMPD5-overexpressing cells exhibited attenuated mitochondrial respiration irrespective of the substrate provided.
source: We measured the activity of the respiratory chain by providing substrates for each respiratory chain complex to permeabilized cells and analyzed oxygen consumption. mtSMPD5-overexpressing cells exhibited attenuated mitochondrial respiration irrespective of the substrate provided (Figure 5G–L), supporting the notion that mitochondrial ceramides induce a generalized defect in mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G–L.

claim: Cells with mtSMPD5 overexpression exhibited increased oxidative stress measured by the redox-sensitive dye MitoSOX.
source: In line with defective mitochondrial function, cells with mtSMPD5 overexpression also exhibited increased oxidative stress (Figure 5M) measured by the redox-sensitive dye MitoSOX.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: No difference in mitochondrial membrane potential was observed across conditions with mtSMPD5 overexpression.
source: Interestingly, no difference in mitochondrial membrane potential was observed across conditions (Figure 5N).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: A total of 2058 unique protein groups were quantified in at least one sample from human muscle biopsies, where 571 were annotated as mitochondrial associated proteins.
source: A total of 2058 unique protein groups were quantified in at least one sample, where 571 were annotated as mitochondrial associated proteins (Human MitoCarta 3.0) (Rath et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data analysis.

claim: After filtering, 492 mitochondrial proteins were reliably quantified across 67 samples from human muscle biopsies.
source: After filtering (proteins in >50% of samples within each group), 492 mitochondrial proteins were reliably quantified across 67 samples (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 16% of all mitochondrial proteins were significantly different between T2D and athletes in human muscle biopsies.
source: For instance, 16% of all mitochondrial proteins were significantly different between T2D and athletes (Figure 6C); however, 56% (45/80) of these proteins were changed by less than 1.5-fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: All detected proteins within Complex I of the ETC were highly correlated with muscle insulin sensitivity in human samples.
source: As a group, all detected proteins within CI of the ETC were highly correlated with muscle insulin sensitivity (p=4e-15) (Figure 6E) and to a lesser extent proteins within CIV (p=0.08) and CV (p=0.09; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: As a group, Complex I proteins were inversely correlated with mitochondrial ceramides in human samples.
source: In line with our previous observations, as a group, CI proteins were inversely correlated with mitochondrial ceramides (p=8e-14) and no association was observed between CII and C18:0 ceramides across samples (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The N and Q modules were the regions with the most negative associated subunits with mitochondria ceramides in human muscle.
source: Consistent with L6-mtSMPD5 myotubes, the N and Q modules were the regions with the most negative associated subunits with mitochondria ceramides in human muscle (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Across the two datasets (L6 and human), Complex I and Complex IV subunits were downregulated after mtSMPD5 overexpression and were negatively associated with C18 ceramides in human samples.
source: We observed that across the two datasets CI and CIV subunits were downregulated after mtSMPD5 overexpression and were negatively associated with C18 ceramides in human samples (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Complex I and Complex IV were positively associated with muscle insulin sensitivity in human samples.
source: In turn, CI and CIV were positively associated with muscle insulin sensitivity (Figure 6I), suggesting that these ETC subunits exhibited a conserved sensitivity to ceramide accumulation with a potential role in insulin sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 6I.
